newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: New S.African constitution entrenches democracy.
newsitem.headline: New S.African constitution entrenches democracy.

text.p: The constitution approved by South Africa's top judges on Wednesday will underpin the social revolution wrought by President Nelson Mandela since voters ousted apartheid in the country's first all-race polls in 1994.
The 140-page document was hammered out in two years of talks between Mandela's African National Congress, his former jailors of the white-led National Party and five smaller parties.

A Bill of Rights entrenches the equality deliberately skewed by hundreds of apartheid laws establishing a racial heirarchy with whites at the top, blacks at the bottom and ethnic Indians and mixed-race Coloureds in between.

In what visiting constitutional experts said during the drafting process was one of the world's most liberal documents, the bill prohibits discrimination on any basis, including race, gender, sexual orientation, physical disability, language or religion.
It establishes a right to life that will prevent a return to capital punishment and a right to freedom that cannot be significantly curtailed even in times of national emergency.

The preamble states as a basic goal of the constitution "...to heal the divisions of the past and establish a society based on democratic values, social justice and fundamental human rights...based on the will of the people and (in which) every citizen is equally protected by law."

Driven largely by the difficulty in bringing parties with very different platforms together, constitution-makers opted for a detailed text that spells out rights and obligations, rather than a more simple statement of principles.

Issues such as the future of white education kept negotiators busy through many long nights as former president F.W. de Klerk's disempowered Afrikaner minority fought to protect cultural icons, such as their Calvinist Afrikaans-language schools.
The approved text does not offer Afrikaners any guarantees, but stops short of forcing the racial or linguistic intergration of their schools.

Clauses covering state finances commit the government to a relatively open system of fiscal government and entrench the independence from political authorities of key institutions including the central Reserve Bank and the Auditor General, who oversees state spending.
The constitution also creates autonomous bodies to monitor the rights of youth and women as well as a Public Protector and a Human Rights Commission.

The first draft offered workers guaranteed trade union rights, but denied individual employers the right to bargain outside a collective context. This was changed in a revision ordered by the Constitutional Court to give employers the right to bargain collectively or individually.
Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi failed in his attempt to entrench sweeping powers for provincial governments and to assure the powers and status of tribal chiefs and elders.
His Inkatha Freedom Party boycotted the votes on both the original text adopted in May and the revised text approved in October and ratified on Wednesday by the Constitutional Court.
The constitution gives provinces exclusive powers over some parochial issues, but gives the central government a veto over issues, such as education, that are covered by national norms.

The 90-member Senate created under the interim constitution will make way for a Council of Provinces designed to protect the rights of regional governments and to give them a voice in some national legislation.
